lesson.title: Days, Months & Dates
lesson.subtitle: lunes, martes, en enero — calendar vocabulary and scheduling meetings

hook.title: The Seven Planets Inside Your Week
hook.content: Look at Monday through Friday in Spanish: every single day is named after a celestial body from Roman astronomy! lunes = Moon-day (lunar), martes = Mars-day (martial), miércoles = Mercury-day, jueves = Jove/Jupiter-day, viernes = Venus-day! Then the weekend arrives from Judeo-Christian history: sábado (Sabbath) and domingo (Latin dies Dominicus, 'Day of the Lord')!

pattern.title: Why Spanish Says 'El Lunes' (Never *En Lunes) for 'On Monday'!
pattern.content: In English, you say 'ON Monday' and 'ON Mondays'. In Spanish, you NEVER use a preposition like *en before a day of the week! Instead, the masculine article el / los does all the work: el lunes = 'on Monday'; los lunes = 'on Mondays / every Monday'! Months, on the other hand, DO take en: en enero ('in January'). Notice also that neither days nor months are capitalized in Spanish!
pattern.linguist_note: Latin diēs Lūnae, Mārtis, Mercuriī, Iovis, Veneris dropped the word diēs while keeping its masculine gender.
pattern.trap_note: Because lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, and viernes already end in unstressed -es, their plural form doesn't change at all: el lunes ('on Monday') → los lunes ('on Mondays')!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: el lunes, el martes, el miércoles, el jueves, el viernes, el sábado / el domingo
exercises.meaning: Monday (Moon-day), Tuesday (Mars-day), Wednesday (Mercury-day), Thursday (Jupiter-day), Friday (Venus-day), Saturday / Sunday
exercises.explanation: All seven days of the week are masculine and written in lowercase.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'I am going to Madrid on Monday' in Spanish?
exercises.meaning: I am going to Madrid on Monday
exercises.explanation: The masculine article el means 'on [weekday]': el lunes.

exercises.meaning: On Friday we are going to celebrate
exercises.explanation: El viernes ('On Friday') + vamos a celebrar ('we are going to celebrate').

exercises.idea: say that you have time this week
cues: this (feminine to match la semana) → esta
exercises.explanation: Tengo tiempo esta semana — la semana is feminine, so 'this week' is esta semana.

exercises.prompt: Which English word-for-word blueprint mirrors Spanish 'El lunes voy a Madrid'?
exercises.natural: On Monday I am going to Madrid
options: On Monday I am going to Madrid
At the Monday going to Madrid
exercises.meaning: On Monday I am going to Madrid (literal Spanish blueprint: The Monday I-go to Madrid)
exercises.explanation: Spanish uses the definite article ('The Monday') where English uses 'On Monday'.

summary.outcome: Name the days of the week, express 'on Monday / on Mondays' with el / los, and use en with months.

use_example.german: El lunes voy a Madrid y el viernes vamos a celebrar.
use_example.english: On Monday I am going to Madrid and on Friday we are going to celebrate.

summary.takeaway: Days of the week take el ('on Monday') and los ('on Mondays') — never *en lunes!
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([1601] The Days of the Planets): see why lunes through viernes stay identical in the plural.

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'In January it is cold (hay frío -> tengo frío)'
twist.explanation: Months take en: En enero tengo frío.

foreshadow.line: Now that you can anchor events on the calendar, Topic 17 unlocks your first past tense: the -ado / -ido past with haber!

payoff.text: Notice how miércoles, jueves, and viernes show the exact same e→ie and o→ue vowel shifts you saw in Topic 15's numbers (siete, nueve, diez)!

lunes.etymology_derivation: Spanish uses the masculine article el/los to mean 'on [weekday]': el lunes ('on Monday'), los lunes ('on Mondays')!

martes.context_translation: We'll see each other on Tuesday.

miércoles.etymology_derivation: Mercury's day, with an esdrújula accent.

viernes.etymology_derivation: Venus's day. All five (lunes–viernes) end in -es and stay unchanged in the plural (el lunes / los lunes)!

sábado.context_translation: On Saturday we're going to the movies.

semana.context_translation: This week I have a lot of work.

enero.etymology_derivation: Months take en ('in'): en enero, en mayo.

el.etymology_derivation: Latin demonstrative ille ('that one') trimmed down over centuries to el. Spanish pointers became articles.
